description: Hey! We're currently a team of 3 high school students, looking to have fun in this local hackathon. Some of us are interested in pursuing astrophysics in the future, while others are looking to develop cool software. We're in need of people with strong technical skills, particularly in programming, AI, and web development.

details:
What it does

Astronautics Flame Lab (AFL) turns NASA’s microgravity fire experiments into something you can explore and question. It reads the public records in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and loads 403 real tests: 129 solid-fuel tests from BASS-II and 274 droplet tests from FLEX. It has four tools:

  • Flame Lab replays any BASS-II test in NASA’s flow duct, with the sample, oxygen, air speed and outcome taken from the test’s record. In the sandbox you set your own conditions and get an estimate counted from NASA’s nearest tests, which you can save and export.
  • Experiment Map plots the tests in 3D, so you can see where NASA has data and where it doesn’t.
  • Find Studies ranks NASA’s combustion investigations for a lunar rover question and shows the evidence gap.
  • Ember, our AI assistant, answers questions from the records and links every claim to its source.

Benefits and intended impact

Fire behaves differently without gravity, and Moon habitats are expected to use air with 30 % oxygen or more. AFL helps students, researchers and engineers find which tests bear on a design question and what they show. It also shows what has never been tested: no solid material in the loaded records was tested at Moon-base air, and PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data. Knowing where the evidence stops is as useful for fire safety as the evidence itself.

How it’s built

  • Python, FastAPI and DuckDB on the back end, hosted on Vercel.
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript on the front end, with Plotly for the 3D map and three.js for the flame lab.
  • Anthropic’s Claude API for Ember.
  • 542 automated tests run on every push.
  • We designed the interface in Figma and built the code with Claude Code during the event.

How it’s creative

Most AI tools guess. Ours is built not to. Code checks every claim Ember writes against the cited NASA record before it is shown, and removes claims that fail. When the data can’t answer, the site says “not enough evidence” and shows the nearest tests NASA did run. The sandbox estimate is a count of how real tests ended, labelled as an estimate, and it says “no estimate” when nothing is close. The drawn flame is always labelled as a drawing.

What we considered

  • Validity first: every number links to its PSI record or NASA report page, and what NASA observed is kept separate from our reading of it.
  • Different readers: three reading levels (Beginner, Simple, Expert) and a 60-second tour for judges.
  • Honest limits: unknown values are never counted as matches, and tests with missing values are counted, not placed by guesswork.
  • Privacy: no accounts, cookies or trackers.
  • Fair play: all code was written during the hackathon. An earlier prototype from November 10 and 13 was set aside and not used.
